Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: Alpha Ltd. holds 22% of the voting power in another company in a fiduciary capacity. It also holds a 35% interest in a joint venture agreement and participates in the decision-making process of the joint venture. Examine whether the company qualifies as an associate company under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
Case Facts / Data: 22% voting power held in fiduciary capacity; 35% interest in a joint venture; participates in joint-venture decision-making.
Chapter: The Companies Act, 2013 — Definitions / Associate Company
Primary Concept: Associate company; significant influence; joint venture; fiduciary capacity
Provision / Section Reference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(6) and its Explanation
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Section 2(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines an associate company, in relation to another company, as a company in which that other company has significant influence but which is not its subsidiary; the term also includes a joint venture company. Significant influence means control of at least 20% of total voting power, or participation in business decisions under an agreement. The 22% voting power stated to be held in a fiduciary capacity should not be relied upon as Alpha Ltd.'s own significant influence. However, Alpha Ltd. has a 35% interest in a joint venture and participates in its decision-making process. The joint venture is expressly included within the definition of associate company. Therefore, on the facts given, the joint venture qualifies as an associate company of Alpha Ltd., provided it is not a subsidiary of Alpha Ltd.
Expected Conclusion: Yes. The joint venture qualifies as an associate company because it is a joint venture in which Alpha Ltd. has a 35% interest and participates in decision-making; the fiduciary holding does not need to be counted.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 2(6) | significant influence | 20% of total voting power | business decisions under an agreement | joint venture company | fiduciary capacity | not a subsidiary
Common Mistakes / Traps: Counting the fiduciary holding as if it were Alpha Ltd.'s own beneficial voting power; omitting that a joint venture is expressly included; treating 20% as the only possible route to significant influence.

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: Zest Services Private Limited is a subsidiary company. Its paid-up share capital is ₹8 crore and its turnover, as per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year, is ₹90 crore. Examine whether Zest Services Private Limited qualifies as a small company under the Companies Act, 2013.
Case Facts / Data: Private company; it is a subsidiary; paid-up share capital ₹8 crore; preceding-year turnover ₹90 crore.
Primary Concept: Small company; financial thresholds; excluded categories
Provision / Section Reference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(85), read with Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014, as amended
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a small company as a company other than a public company that satisfies the prescribed paid-up share capital and turnover limits. However, the proviso expressly excludes a holding company and a subsidiary company, among other categories, from the definition. Zest Services Private Limited is stated to be a subsidiary company and is therefore excluded from the definition of a small company, irrespective of its financial figures. For context, from 1 December 2025 the prescribed limits were increased to paid-up share capital not exceeding ₹10 crore and turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore. Zest's figures fall within those current limits, but the subsidiary-company exclusion still prevents it from qualifying. If the question is intended for an examination attempt before 1 December 2025, the then-applicable lower limits also need to be considered; the subsidiary exclusion remains decisive in either case.
Expected Conclusion: No. Zest Services Private Limited is a subsidiary company, which is expressly excluded from the definition of a small company under Section 2(85).
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 2(85) | other than a public company | prescribed paid-up capital and turnover limits | subsidiary company excluded | proviso
Common Mistakes / Traps: Answering only by comparing capital and turnover; overlooking the express exclusion of subsidiary companies; applying current thresholds to a historical examination question without checking the relevant date.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, page 1; Section 2(85); MCA/PIB update on revised thresholds effective 1 December 2025.

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: Aman is already a member of one One Person Company (OPC). On the death of another OPC member on 1 October 2023, Aman becomes a member of that OPC as well. Examine whether Aman can continue as a member of both OPCs and state the time limit, if any, within which he must comply with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
Case Facts / Data: Aman is already an OPC member; on 1 October 2023 he becomes member of a second OPC on the death of its member, apparently as nominee.
Chapter: The Companies Act, 2013 — Incorporation and allied matters
Primary Concept: OPC membership restriction; nominee succeeding to membership; 180-day compliance period
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Rule 3(2) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 provides that a natural person shall not be a member of more than one One Person Company at any point of time and shall not be a nominee of more than one such company. Rule 3(3) provides an exception where a person who is a member of one OPC becomes a member of another OPC by virtue of being a nominee in that company. In such a case, the person must meet the eligibility requirement within 180 days. Accordingly, Aman cannot continue as a member of both OPCs beyond the permitted period. He must choose one OPC and cease to be a member of the other within 180 days from becoming a member of the second OPC. If the membership arose on 1 October 2023, the 180-day period would ordinarily run to 29 March 2024, subject to the applicable rules of date computation.
Expected Conclusion: Aman cannot continue as a member of both OPCs indefinitely. He must regularise his membership within 180 days of becoming a member of the second OPC.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Rule 3(2) | Rule 3(3) | natural person | not a member of more than one OPC | nominee | 180 days | choose one OPC
Common Mistakes / Traps: Saying there is no time to regularise the situation; confusing the 180-day exception with a permanent right to hold membership in two OPCs; omitting that the second membership arises by nomination.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, page 2; Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, Rule 3(2)–(3).

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: Explain the provisions relating to the reservation of the name of a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) under Section 16 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, with reference to: (i) the circumstances in which an application for reservation of a name may be made; (ii) the form and fee requirements; (iii) the period for which the name may be reserved; and (iv) restrictions relating to undesirable or identical names.
Case Facts / Data: Explain four specified aspects of LLP name reservation.
Primary Concept: Reservation of LLP name; RUN-LLP; name restrictions; validity period
Provision / Section Reference: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, Sections 15 and 16; Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009, Rule 18 and current MCA RUN-LLP instructions
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Under Section 16 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, a person may apply to the Registrar for reservation of (a) the name of a proposed LLP, or (b) a new name to which an existing LLP proposes to change its name. The application is made electronically through the prescribed MCA process, commonly the RUN-LLP (Reserve Unique Name–LLP) service, with the prescribed fee; the current normal fee shown in MCA instructions is ₹200 per application. Under Section 16(2), if the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed name is not liable to be rejected under Section 15(2), the Registrar may reserve it for three months from the date of intimation. A name may be refused if it is undesirable or identical with, or too nearly resembles, the name of another LLP or company, or conflicts with a registered trade mark or other applicable naming restrictions. The proposed name must therefore satisfy the statutory and prescribed naming conditions.
Expected Conclusion: A proposed or changed LLP name can be reserved through the prescribed MCA process for three months, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with the statutory restrictions on names.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 16 | proposed LLP | change of name of existing LLP | RUN-LLP | prescribed fee | ₹200 | three months | Section 15(2) | undesirable | identical or too nearly resembles | registered trade mark
Common Mistakes / Traps: Stating a validity period of 60 or 90 days instead of the statutory three months; omitting the existing-LLP name-change route; treating payment of the fee as guaranteeing approval.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, pages 2–3; LLP Act Sections 15–16; MCA RUN-LLP instruction kit and fee details.

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: Mr. Aman, a partner of an LLP, has provided useful information during an investigation. A penalty of ₹1,25,000 has been imposed on him. He is also an employee of the LLP. Answer with reference to Section 31 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008: (i) Can the Tribunal waive or reduce the penalty imposed on Mr. Aman? (ii) Can the LLP discharge, terminate or otherwise penalise him in his capacity as an employee for providing such information?
Case Facts / Data: Aman is an LLP partner and employee; provided useful information during investigation; penalty ₹1,25,000.
Chapter: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 — Liability and whistle-blowing
Primary Concept: Whistle-blowing; waiver/reduction of penalty; protection from employment discrimination
Model Answer (Exam-ready): (i) Yes. Under Section 31(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, the Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive any penalty leviable against a partner or employee of an LLP if it is satisfied that the person provided useful information during an investigation of the LLP, or that information given by the person leads to a conviction of the LLP or a partner/employee under the LLP Act or any other Act. Since Aman provided useful information during an investigation, the Tribunal may exercise this discretion to reduce or waive the penalty. Waiver or reduction is discretionary, not automatic. (ii) No. Section 31(2) protects a partner or employee from being discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of the LLP relationship or employment merely because the person provided, or caused to be provided, information under Section 31(1). Therefore, the LLP cannot terminate or penalise Aman in his capacity as an employee merely for providing that information.
Expected Conclusion: The Tribunal may waive or reduce the ₹1,25,000 penalty, but it is discretionary. The LLP must not discharge or discriminate against Aman in his employment merely because he provided information under Section 31.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 31(1) | Court or Tribunal | may reduce or waive | useful information during investigation | discretionary | Section 31(2) | discharged | demoted | suspended | threatened | harassed | discriminated against
Common Mistakes / Traps: Treating waiver as automatic; omitting the alternative conviction-based route in Section 31(1); stating the LLP may terminate him simply because he is also a partner; overlooking the employment protection.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, pages 3–4; LLP Act, Section 31 (Whistle blowing).

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: A company received application money from its members on 20 March 2023 for the issue of securities through private placement. However, the company failed to allot the securities by 30 June 2023. Examine the validity of the members' objection regarding non-allotment of securities and determine whether they are entitled to claim interest on the application money. Support your answer with reference to Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Case Facts / Data: Application money received 20 March 2023 for private placement; securities not allotted by 30 June 2023.
Chapter: The Companies Act, 2013 — Prospectus and Allotment of Securities
Primary Concept: Private placement; allotment deadline; refund; interest on delayed refund
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a company making a private placement to allot the securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money. If it is unable to allot within that period, it must repay the application money within 15 days from expiry of the 60-day period. If the company fails to repay within that additional 15-day period, it is liable to repay the money with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the sixtieth day. Here, the money was received on 20 March 2023 and securities had not been allotted by 30 June 2023, well beyond the 60-day allotment period. The members' objection is therefore valid. If the application money was not refunded within the further 15-day period, the subscribers are entitled to repayment with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the 60th day. Assuming the date of receipt is excluded in counting, the 60-day period ended on 19 May 2023 and the further 15-day refund period ended on 3 June 2023.
Expected Conclusion: The objection is valid. If the company did not refund within the additional 15 days after the 60-day period, the subscribers are entitled to 12% p.a. interest from expiry of the 60th day.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 42(6) | private placement | within 60 days | repay within 15 days | expiry of sixtieth day | 12% per annum | valid objection
Common Mistakes / Traps: Starting the 12% interest only after the additional 15 days; confusing the 60-day allotment deadline with the 15-day refund period; overlooking that interest applies if refund is not made in the further 15 days.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, pages 4–5; Companies Act, 2013, Section 42(6).

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: A company has the following balances: Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) ₹1,50,000; Securities Premium ₹90,000; Surplus in Statement of Profit and Loss ₹1,20,000; total ₹3,60,000. The company proposes to issue bonus shares in the ratio of 1:3. The face value of each share is ₹10 and there are 90,000 existing shares. (a) Identify the sources from which the company may issue bonus shares under Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013. (b) Calculate the number and amount of bonus shares to be issued. (c) Can the company issue bonus shares before making the final call on partly paid-up shares? Explain.
Case Facts / Data: CRR ₹1,50,000; securities premium ₹90,000; P&L surplus ₹1,20,000; total reserves ₹3,60,000; bonus ratio 1:3; face value ₹10; existing shares 90,000.
Chapter: The Companies Act, 2013 — Share Capital and Debentures
Primary Concept: Sources and conditions for issue of bonus shares; bonus calculation; partly paid-up shares
Provision / Section Reference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 63(1)–(3); Section 52(2)(a) for permitted use of securities premium
Model Answer (Exam-ready): (a) Under Section 63(1), fully paid-up bonus shares may be issued out of: (i) free reserves; (ii) the securities premium account; or (iii) the capital redemption reserve account. Reserves created by revaluation of assets cannot be capitalised for issuing bonus shares. (b) A 1:3 bonus ratio means one bonus share for every three existing shares. Number of bonus shares = 90,000 ÷ 3 = 30,000 shares. Amount of bonus issue = 30,000 × ₹10 face value = ₹3,00,000. The stated balances total ₹3,60,000, which is sufficient, assuming the P&L surplus is available as a free reserve and the other statutory conditions are met. For illustration, the company could capitalise ₹1,50,000 from CRR, ₹90,000 from securities premium and ₹60,000 from eligible P&L surplus. (c) No. Under Section 63(2)(e), the company cannot capitalise profits or reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares unless any partly paid-up shares outstanding on the date of allotment are made fully paid-up. Therefore, the final call must be made and the partly paid-up shares must be fully paid before the bonus shares are allotted.
Expected Conclusion: Permitted sources are free reserves, securities premium and CRR (not revaluation reserves). The company would issue 30,000 bonus shares of ₹10 each, amounting to ₹3,00,000. Any outstanding partly paid-up shares must be made fully paid before allotment.
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Section 63(1) | free reserves | securities premium account | capital redemption reserve | not revaluation reserves | 1:3 | 30,000 shares | ₹3,00,000 | Section 63(2)(e) | partly paid-up shares made fully paid-up
Common Mistakes / Traps: Dividing existing shares by 1 instead of 3; confusing number of bonus shares with rupee amount; using revaluation reserve; stating bonus shares may be issued before partly paid-up shares are fully paid.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, pages 5–6; Companies Act, 2013, Section 63.

Subject: Corporate and Other Laws
Original Question: A company received ₹3,00,000 as application money towards the subscription of securities. The company failed to allot the securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money and also failed to refund the amount within the prescribed additional 15 days. Examine whether the amount received will be treated as a deposit under the Companies Act, 2013.
Case Facts / Data: ₹3,00,000 application money; no allotment within 60 days; no refund within additional 15 days.
Chapter: The Companies Act, 2013 — Acceptance of Deposits / Allotment of Securities
Primary Concept: Application money deemed deposit; allotment and refund deadlines
Provision / Section Reference: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, Rule 2(1)(c)(vii), Explanation; Companies Act, 2013, Section 42(6) where the offer is by private placement
Model Answer (Exam-ready): Under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, application money or an advance received towards subscription of securities is excluded from the definition of deposit while the statutory conditions are met. The Explanation provides that such amount is deemed to be a deposit if securities are not allotted within 60 days of receipt of the application money or advance and the amount is not refunded to subscribers within 15 days from expiry of those 60 days. In this case, the company neither allotted the securities within 60 days nor refunded ₹3,00,000 within the further 15-day period. Therefore, the amount is treated as a deposit under the said Rule. If the transaction is a private placement governed by Section 42, the company may also be liable to repay the amount with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the 60th day under Section 42(6).
Expected Conclusion: Yes. Since the securities were not allotted within 60 days and the application money was not refunded within the additional 15 days, ₹3,00,000 is deemed to be a deposit under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii).
Mandatory Keywords / Key Phrases: Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) | application money | not allotted within 60 days | not refunded within 15 days | deemed to be a deposit | Section 42(6) | 12% per annum
Common Mistakes / Traps: Saying the amount becomes a deposit immediately after 60 days without considering the additional 15-day refund period; citing only Section 42 without the Deposits Rules; omitting the conditional interest consequence.
Source Reference: User-uploaded scan, pages 6–7; Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, Rule 2(1)(c)(vii); Companies Act, Section 42(6).
